ethiopia.summary: Mastercard has announced the introduction of advanced AI and tokenization technologies to bolster digital payment security in Ethiopia. This initiative aims to enhance the safety and efficiency of online transactions, addressing the growing concerns over digital fraud and cyber threats. By implementing tokenization, Mastercard will replace sensitive payment information with unique identification symbols, ensuring that actual card details are not exposed during transactions. This move is part of Mastercard's broader strategy to support the digital economy in Ethiopia, which is experiencing rapid growth in e-commerce and mobile payments. The company emphasizes that these innovations will not only protect consumers but also foster trust in digital payment systems, encouraging more users to engage in online financial activities. Mastercard's efforts align with the Ethiopian government's goals to promote financial inclusion and digital transformation across the country.

ethiopia.title: Drought, Food Shortages and Child Malnutrition Deepen Humanitarian Needs in Afar, Amhara and Tigray
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: Drought, Food Shortages and Child Malnutrition Deepen Humanitarian Needs in Afar, Amhara and Tigray - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: Drought, Food Shortages and Child Malnutrition Deepen Humanitarian Needs in Afar, Amhara and Tigray World Food Programme South Omo zone in Ethiopia is facing a severe drought (file photo) 27 October 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) Addis Abeba — Drought, rising food prices, shortages of essential medicines and disruptions to health services are compounding humanitarian needs across northern Ethiopia's Afar , Amhara and Tigray regions , with displaced children particularly vulnerable to acute malnutrition, according to a humanitarian assessment document seen by Addis Standard. The assessment, dated October 19 and covering developments between October 12 and 19, warns that the humanitarian consequences of escalating insecurity are unfolding against a backdrop of unmet needs left by the 2020-2022 northern Ethiopia conflict, subsequent episodes of fighting and displacement, and El Niño-related drought. "Needs are likely to remain high," the assessment states, noting that the combined pressures have compounded existing humanitarian vulnerabilities across Tigray, Amhara and Afar. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn One of the clearest indicators of the crisis is the nutritional situation among displaced children in Tigray. Screening conducted in September and October in Laelay Adiabo, Axum and Adwa found that approximately 15% of around 11,800 children screened in internally displaced communities had moderate acute malnutrition. The assessment cautions that information on the overall scale and severity of humanitarian needs remains fragmented. "At the time of writing, there is no needs assessment data available," it states, identifying rapid humanitarian needs assessments as a priority as access improves. Food insecurity is being aggravated by crop failures, dwindling household resources and rising prices. In Raya Azebo woreda in southern Tigray, drought has devastated agricultural production, leaving households struggling to afford basic food. More than 15,000 of the woreda's 26,000 hectares of farmland had reportedly been cultivated, but only around 400 hectares showed crop growth, according to the assessment. Approximately 10,000 hectares were not planted because of a lack of rainfall in May. A farmer quoted in the assessment said households could no longer afford basic food as prices soared while agricultural production collapsed. Many had exhausted their savings after almost a year without a meaningful harvest. Livestock owners have also suffered as animal prices fell, buyers became scarce, and livestock died from a lack of fodder and disease. Earlier this month, FEWS NET projected Crisis-level food insecurity outcomes, classified as IPC Phase 3 , will persist until January 2027 in parts of southern and eastern Tigray and lowland areas along the Tekeze River catchment. Health services under pressure The crisis is also straining an already fragile healthcare system. Hospitals in Sheraro are reportedly struggling to maintain services amid insecurity, shortages of medical supplies and prolonged delays in salary payments to civil servants. The assessment says unpaid salaries have contributed to health workers leaving the area, further reducing the availability of care. Transporting medical supplies through areas affected by fighting remains difficult, while insecurity is limiting civilians' ability to reach health facilities. Hospitals and other health facilities in Wukro and Adwa, as well as at Adigrat University, have reportedly been looted or vandalized. A cholera outbreak in Wag Hamra zone in Amhara remains a concern, with humanitarian sources reporting limited availability of treatment supplies, including fluids. Mental health needs in conflict-affected parts of Afar also remain high, the assessment notes. There have, however, been signs of improvement in humanitarian access to Tigray. An inter-agency convoy delivered essential supplies, including medicines, to northern Ethiopia on October 14, while the World Health Organization dispatched more than 71 tons of medical supplies. Hospitals in Tigray have also begun resuming operations. The resumption of humanitarian flights to Mekelle and increased movement along the Semera-Abaala-Mekelle corridor have helped humanitarian organizations move personnel and supplies into the region. The International Committee of the Red Cross and the Ethiopian Red Cross Society also delivered essential equipment and medicines to hospitals in Shire, Maichew, Mekhoni and Alamata, as well as Chercher Health Centre. Despite these developments, the assessment warns that access remains difficult or unsafe in areas experiencing active hostilities. In Amhara, road blockages and insecurity continue to delay convoy movements, while humanitarian personnel have reportedly faced harassment, theft and demands for money. Displacement and access to basic necessities Displacement across Tigray, Afar and Amhara has largely remained within the same districts or zones, according to the assessment. However, the scale of new movements remains uncertain. Civilians in rural parts of northwestern Tigray have reportedly moved toward Shire amid ongoing hostilities and heavy artillery fire. The assessment warns that new arrivals could intensify pressure on shelter and services in areas already hosting large internally displaced populations. In Afar, an estimated 11,000 to 13,000 people may remain displaced, although the figures are difficult to verify. Some people previously displaced from areas including Abaala and Megale have reportedly returned home as security and humanitarian access improved. In Zala Anbesa, few supplies were reportedly reaching the town as of October 15, prices were rising sharply, and shops, restaurants and other businesses had closed, affecting both livelihoods and access to basic necessities. The assessment warns that continued or intensified fighting could further undermine food security by restricting market supplies, prolonging shortages of cash and fuel, and driving up staple food prices. Education has also been disrupted. Schools in Erob, Gulo Mekeda and Zala Anbesa in eastern Tigray remain closed, while the reported use of school facilities by armed actors in Tahtay Koraro has interrupted classes during the school year. The full extent of the humanitarian crisis remains difficult to establish because of limited access, incomplete information and disrupted administrative structures. In Tigray, interruptions to the regional agriculture and disaster risk management institutions have also weakened local capacity to respond to drought. The assessment concludes that improving humanitarian access must be accompanied by rapid needs assessments and stronger coordination to establish the scale of unmet needs and guide the response. It notes that the absence of functioning administrative structures continues to complicate humanitarian planning and coordination. Read the original article on Addis Standard . ethiopia.summary: A recent humanitarian assessment highlights the escalating crisis in Ethiopia's Afar, Amhara, and Tigray regions, exacerbated by severe drought, food shortages, and rising child malnutrition rates. The report, dated October 19, reveals that approximately 15% of 11,800 screened children in internally displaced communities in Tigray suffer from moderate acute malnutrition. The ongoing conflict and El Niño-related drought have compounded existing vulnerabilities, leading to significant food insecurity, particularly in southern Tigray, where crop failures have devastated agricultural production. Health services are under severe strain due to insecurity, shortages of medical supplies, and unpaid salaries, causing health workers to leave. Displacement remains a critical issue, with many civilians moving towards Shire amid ongoing hostilities. The assessment emphasizes the urgent need for improved humanitarian access and rapid needs assessments to address the fragmented information and guide responses effectively. Despite some improvements in access, challenges persist, complicating the humanitarian situation further.

ethiopia.title: Liberation Without Domination - Ethiopia's Opposition Alliance and the Right to Decide
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: Liberation Without Domination - Ethiopia's Opposition Alliance and the Right to Decide - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: Liberation Without Domination - Ethiopia's Opposition Alliance and the Right to Decide 27 October 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) opinion By Dr. Hambisa Belina Addis Abeba — The Ethiopian Peoples' Forces Alliance for Survival, or EPFAS, was announced on 20 September 2026. Announced participants included the Oromo Liberation Front-Oromo Liberation Army, known as OLF-OLA, the Amhara Fano National Movement, and the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF). Its statement , reproduced on an OLF-OLA-associated website, proposes an inclusive temporary government, temporary governing rules, and public discussion of the country's political future. The central issue is political authorship: people's continuing power to shape, approve, challenge, and revise the rules and institutions governing their lives. It must operate throughout the struggle and transition. A promised future vote does not, by itself, authorize the powers leaders exercise beforehand. Domination means exposure to power people cannot effectively contest or control, even when no mistreatment occurs and leaders promise to act wisely. Republican political thought calls freedom from this vulnerability non-domination. Applied reciprocally, it protects communities against imposed arrangements and individuals against unchecked authority within them. Neither legal office nor a liberation claim excuses unchecked power. Political authorship makes power answerable at both levels. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn Cooperation among former enemies may help stop fighting and enable negotiation. It also raises questions about representation, civilian safety, and governing powers. Incumbents must face the same scrutiny. Existing institutions carry legal responsibilities an opposition statement cannot set aside. Holding office does not excuse ruling through fear; opposing a government does not establish a right to replace it. Different decisions need different permission Three levels of authorization matter. Organizational authorization is a mandate from a movement's members or appropriate internal body, including permission to join an alliance. Alliance authorization concerns participating organizations' rules and limits for cooperation. Constituent authorization comes from the people bound by decisions about their political status or constitutional future. Authority at one level does not automatically confer authority at another. Temporary government also needs separate public authorization and a lawful basis for its powers. Joining an alliance need not require a referendum. Negotiators may arrange a ceasefire without authority to decide borders, appoint a government, or settle whether a people remains in a federation or becomes independent. Each decision needs authority appropriate to its consequences. The available public documents, examined through 14 October 2026, record promises of public choice alongside objections and contested participation. ACLED reported that the Gumuz movement denied joining and that rival Ogaden National Liberation Front factions disputed participation. Published reactions also differ. Advocacy for Oromia rejected EPFAS, arguing that it inadequately addressed Oromo grievances and historical redress. T. M. Asfaw opposed cooperation over divergent political projects and risks to Fano's cohesion; Habte H. urged that EPFAS be judged by civilian protection and the accountability of any transitional government. These positions raise questions for leaders; none measures public opinion. The reviewed documents do not establish specific instructions authorizing representatives to join EPFAS or agreed public procedures for approving temporary appointments and governing powers. Nor do they establish an agreed alliance choice among federation, a negotiated political relationship, and independence for Oromia or other peoples. Undisclosed arrangements cannot simply be presumed absent, but the public needs more than assurances. A promised future vote does not, by itself, authorize the powers leaders exercise beforehand." The statements and interviews reviewed here do not establish what most of the Oromo, Amharas, Tigrayans, or others want. Support for a movement, its alliance, and a particular settlement are separate questions. Leaders must discover those differences and let them affect decisions. Listening must be able to change decisions The Brazilian educator Paulo Freire offers a demanding understanding of liberation. People must take part in understanding their circumstances and shaping the effort to change them. Leaders have to learn from those experiences, explain their own thinking, and revise it through dialogue. Reflection and action belong together: people and leaders act, examine the consequences, and learn how to proceed. Frantz Fanon warned that liberation could replace officeholders while ordinary people remained excluded from governing. Freire offers a response: leaders and communities learn through dialogue, and public criticism must be able to change strategy and the terms of delegated authority. Listening helps a struggle avoid reproducing the domination it opposes. Engagement must begin while choices remain open and continue throughout the struggle. Meetings held only after decisions are settled give people little influence. Leaders should explain which proposals changed because people challenged them and give reasons for rejecting others. A community may be concerned about unsafe roads, missing relatives, or farmland access, while its leaders prioritize an alliance. Engagement must address both sets of concerns. Usable information and independent space to propose alternatives can reveal dangers or priorities leaders have overlooked. The OLF-OLA's 2023 manifesto affirms Oromo self-determination and freely elected representatives. Its members' approval cannot substitute for the choices of everyone it claims to represent. Leaders' interests and public preferences may differ; continuing engagement helps expose and address that difference. The Oromo Liberation Front--Adda Bilisummaa Oromoo (ABO) in Afaan Oromo--reported adopting a political program at its August 2017 congress . The program, according to a nonpublic copy consulted by the author, advocated an independent Oromia while pledging to respect the Oromo people's decision on self-determination and making political association conditional on public choice. It records an organizational position at that time; it does not establish present public preferences or an EPFAS-specific mandate for today's OLF-OLA. Advocating a constitutional outcome does not, by itself, give an organization authority to decide that outcome for the people. In the BBC's Afaan Oromo interview account , adviser Jireenyaa Guddataa describes procedural cooperation rather than a merger, with organizations retaining separate leadership, programs, and forces. He says the public should decide unresolved political questions. These explanations clarify the movement's position; they do not establish agreed alliance rules or public approval. Operational secrecy may protect lives but needs specific reasons, limited scope, and independent review. It cannot justify blanket secrecy about political commitments or postponing accountability until victory. People must be able to criticize strategy without being branded enemies of the struggle. Discussion must reach people outside party structures and those pushed out of public life. Women, young people, displaced families, farmers, pastoralists, workers, and minority residents need safe opportunities to shape what gets discussed. Commanders, donors, officials, and customary leaders should not control who gets heard. Five questions can turn the principles of non-domination and leadership through dialogue into a practical test of political authorship: Who claims to speak on whose behalf? Who has granted them the authority to make decisions, what decisions are they authorized to make, and for how long? Can those affected raise their own priorities and challenge proposals without fear of reprisal? How will each decision be approved through a fair process? Finally, how can people challenge a wrong, replace their representatives, or reclaim powers they have delegated? Freedom for Oromia must protect everyone Reciprocal non-domination requires the Oromo people's real authority over political arrangements and protection against arbitrary power for every individual in Oromia. Equal rights belong to everyone, regardless of ethnicity, gender, religion, political affiliation, or social status. Political authorship gives people continuing control over governing institutions; equal rights limit even publicly authorized leaders. An Oromo-led government can still dominate residents who cannot effectively challenge its decisions. The principle extends across communities. Those demanding freedom from imposed rule must respect other peoples' corresponding freedom. No alliance vote gives one movement authority to decide another people's status or settle a disputed territory by military force. Respect for these rights must not depend on an opponent showing the same restraint. A reformed federation, a new agreed political relationship among peoples, and independence for Oromia or other peoples must remain open to peaceful debate. Ethiopia's Constitution recognizes self-determination, including the right to form an independent state, and sets procedures for exercising it. It also protects equality and political participation. Collective rights and residents' individual rights both matter. Article 39(4) specifies how secession may be exercised: a demand approved by two-thirds of the legislative council of the people concerned, a federally organized referendum within three years of the federal government receiving the council's decision, and, if a majority supports secession, transfer of powers and division of assets as prescribed by law. Border disputes and constitutional amendments have separate procedures. Following these procedures does not, by itself, eliminate coercion or exclusion, but neither an alliance agreement nor military control substitutes for a lawful constituent decision. The Oromo people's collective rights, Oromia's governmental powers, and residents' individual rights are connected but distinct. Rules for selecting delegates or voters must be publicly explained, respect collective rights, protect residents and displaced people, and allow independent challenges. Neither control of a disputed area nor forced displacement may determine whose voice counts. Shared institutions may be needed for security, revenues, transport, and public services. Their powers should be agreed, limited, and open to challenge. This does not give every local leader a veto over ordinary common decisions. Fair procedures can produce binding decisions despite disagreement, while protecting those who lose a vote. Political authorship concerns who may exercise authority and how people hold it answerable. Reciprocal non-domination limits every actor's conduct, authorized or not. Civilian protection is an immediate obligation. Civilian protection cannot wait ACLED reported that an August 2026 ambush by the Bizamo Command in western Oromia killed at least sixteen people, including eleven civilians and five soldiers. It also reported that the Amhara Fano National Movement, later announced as an EPFAS participant, claimed Bizamo fell under its command. How can OLF-OLA justify cooperation with a partner claiming command over a unit implicated in killing civilians in Oromia? Each partner must prevent forces under its control from attacking civilians, including those another partner claims to represent, and support independent investigation and accountability. Scrutiny must also reach OLF-OLA. Amnesty International's 2026 briefing documented ten survivors' accounts of sexual violence in western Oromia, supported by medical evidence. Survivors identified OLF-OLA fighters; one also identified an Ethiopian army soldier. Amnesty could not verify the named individuals' identities. These accounts demand survivor protection and independent investigation, without assigning guilt to an entire organization. OLF-OLA's manifesto calls for independent investigation. In the BBC account, Guddataa disputes allegations against the movement while pledging punishment of offenders under its control. These statements require independent testing; the manifesto's general commitments are not a specific response to Amnesty's later findings. Government authority likewise requires scrutiny. Human Rights Watch's 2026 country report , covering 2025, describes abuses during armed conflict and government repression of independent media and civil society. A 2024 Reuters investigation reported extrajudicial killings and unlawful detention linked to Oromia's Koree Nageenyaa security committee. The same investigation reported that the Ethiopian Human Rights Commission's head confirmed the committee's existence and said it had exceeded its mandate. Liberation without a new dominator means that those acting in the people's name remain within the people's reach." Holding all actors to standards of protection does not mean that every allegation rests on equally strong evidence or that responsibility is equal. Every force must prevent attacks on civilians, sexual violence, forced displacement, child recruitment, and obstruction of relief. Survivors need care, safe reporting, and access to justice. These duties apply immediately, whether or not an actor has public permission to govern. Temporary power needs limits from the start A future vote cannot automatically authorize everything leaders do before it. Temporary administrations may shape constitutional choice by appointing officials, selecting participants, controlling security, or narrowing the options people may debate. Before exercising discretionary power, a temporary administration needs a publicly approved mandate. People must know who selected it, who approved its powers, what it may do, and when its authority expires. Independent civilian oversight and legal review must enable changes to appointments or decisions. Where safe elections are impossible, temporary arrangements need open selection rules, nominations from political, community, and independent civic groups, protected objections, and early public review. Authority must remain limited, and successful challenges must be able to change appointments or mandates. Calling a body inclusive establishes neither representation of everyone nor authority to decide the constitutional future. Who authorizes the body setting these selection rules? Publicly justified procedures involving affected communities' representatives and diverse civic groups must determine its membership and mandates. Minorities, displaced people, and politically unaffiliated residents must have a protected right to participate. Those procedures must also face independent legal review. A civilian body can help legally authorized institutions develop separate procedures for consultation, delegate selection, and referendum eligibility. Calling itself representative confers no authority to make binding rules. Without a full public mandate, provisional authority must remain especially narrow, temporary, and reviewable. Different tasks require different thresholds. Ceasefire talks, relief access, and indispensable services may proceed lawfully under narrow, reviewable powers without a constituent vote. Governing appointments, security, and budgets need time-limited public authorization and lawful authority. Final status and foundational constitutional arrangements require constituent decisions. Urgency creates no general license to govern. There was a problem processing your submission. Please try again later. Public approval and legal authority differ. Article 9(3) of Ethiopia's Constitution prohibits assuming state power outside constitutional procedures. The African Charter on Democracy, Elections and Governance , ratified by Ethiopia, treats replacement of a democratically elected government by armed dissidents or rebels as unconstitutional; application depends on the government's democratic character and particular facts. Neither victory nor public support alone makes an administration lawful. Lawfully holding public office does not justify coercion or the permanent denial of recognized rights. Where institutions obstruct those rights, negotiated constitutional change requires disclosed negotiating mandates, an account of the obstruction and legal status, and protection of competing choices. Obstruction does not transfer constituent authority to commanders. Peace must reach everyday life Political authorship also matters in decisions about land, livelihoods, resources, and everyday life, beyond governments and constitutions. Oromo political thought helps connect these safeguards to everyday relationships. Safuu holds those in authority accountable to standards of restraint, dignity, and responsibility toward others and the living environment. Gadaa's traditions of deliberation and succession offer lessons about limited office and public assessment of leaders. Women's institutions such as Siiqqee also express capacities to organize and challenge wrongdoing. These traditions vary and have changed over time. Historical gender and status inequalities require critical scrutiny. Contemporary institutions drawing on them must protect equal rights and remain answerable to residents with different beliefs. Nagaa connects peace with just coexistence among people and their surroundings. Applied to a political settlement, it directs attention to whether displaced families can return safely, livelihoods can recover, water is clean, and injuries receive a fair hearing. A ceasefire deserves protection even while that work remains unfinished. Together, Safuu, Gadaa, and Nagaa connect political authorship to ethical restraint, public review of officeholders, and material repair. They deepen Freire's demand for continuing public control: even a government chosen through fair procedures can dominate when decisions affecting land, livelihoods, or the environment remain beyond effective challenge. This tests promises of change: people need meaningful influence over land, mining, development, and public money, with effective ways to challenge harm. The proposed Addis Ababa-Oromia Master Plan raised fears that capital expansion would displace Oromo farmers. Protests met a violent crackdown; the plan was canceled in January 2016. That reversal showed protest could change policy; it did not establish lasting public control over land. Replacing officeholders can leave familiar power intact if land and resource decisions remain beyond public control. EPFAS should be judged by the powers it claims and decisions it makes, with the same scrutiny applied to incumbents and other actors. Political authorship must extend through struggle, temporary government, and final settlement, with people able to authorize decisions, challenge them, and secure change through fair procedures. Liberation without a new dominator means that those acting in the people's name remain within the people's reach. AS Editor's Note : Dr. Hambisa Belina is an associate professor of accounting
ethiopia.summary: The Ethiopian Peoples' Forces Alliance for Survival (EPFAS), formed on September 20, 2026, includes the Oromo Liberation Front-Oromo Liberation Army (OLF-OLA), the Amhara Fano National Movement, and the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF). The alliance advocates for an inclusive temporary government and emphasizes the importance of political authorship, where the people retain the power to shape their governance. The article critiques the potential for domination within this alliance, arguing that authority must be derived from the people and that leaders should be accountable to their constituents. It highlights the need for ongoing public engagement and dialogue to ensure that diverse voices, including marginalized groups, are heard in decision-making processes. The article also stresses that any political arrangements must respect the rights of all ethnic groups and individuals, advocating for a lawful approach to self-determination and governance in Ethiopia. Ultimately, it calls for a political environment where power is answerable and non-domination is prioritized.

ethiopia.title: More Than 60 Killed in Oromia as Ethiopia’s Instability Deepens, Raising Alarm for Mogadishu - FTL Somalia
ethiopia.content: More Than 60 Killed in Oromia as Ethiopia's Instability Deepens, Raising Alarm for Mogadishu - Somali News today Live Home Politics Security Elections More News Premium Economy & Business Education Entertainment & Lifestyle Environment & Climate Health International Relations Technology & Innovation Sports News By Region Nationwide Benadir Galmudug Hirshabelle Jubaland Puntland South West State Somaliland North Eastern State Resources Infographics Downloads Videos FAQ About Somalia Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Home Politics Security Elections More News Premium Economy & Business Education Entertainment & Lifestyle Environment & Climate Health International Relations Technology & Innovation Sports News By Region Nationwide Benadir Galmudug Hirshabelle Jubaland Puntland South West State Somaliland North Eastern State Resources Infographics Downloads Videos FAQ About Somalia Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Security Nationwide More Than 60 Killed in Oromia as Ethiopia’s Instability Deepens, Raising Alarm for Mogadishu October 27, 2026 6 min read MOGADISHU , The massacre of more than 60 Christians in Ethiopia’s Oromia region is not a distant tragedy for Somalia. It is a direct indicator of the escalating instability in a neighboring state whose internal conflicts are increasingly intertwined with Somalia’s own security and political trajectory. A Pattern of Sectarian Violence According to the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, more than 60 people were killed in attacks on three areas in the Shirka district of Oromia. A local official blamed the Alliance for Survival, a newly formed rebel coalition that includes the Oromo Liberation Army (OLA). The OLA has denied involvement in previous such attacks. Eyewitnesses told BBC Amharic that five of those killed were children, and that 20 houses were burned to the ground. The Ethiopian Human Rights Council reported in July 2026 that 458 people had been killed in attacks in that area over the previous four years, describing them as religiously motivated and targeting followers of the Orthodox Church. This latest massacre is one of the deadliest in that period. The Rebel Alliance Behind the Chaos The Shirka killings are part of a wider pattern of escalating violence across Ethiopia. A coalition of seven armed groups, including the TPLF, the Fano militia in Amhara, and the OLA, has announced the formation of the Ethiopian Peoples’ Forces Alliance for Survival, aimed at removing Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s government. As reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the alliance , the coalition spans half of Ethiopia’s twelve regional states and brings together groups that have previously fought one another, making the alignment an unusual development in the country’s fragmented opposition landscape. The Ogaden National Liberation Front (ONLF), a Somali-majority armed group, is among the signatories. Its inclusion is particularly notable given the group’s 2018 peace agreement with the Ethiopian government and its subsequent focus on diplomatic efforts to advance the interests of ethnic Somalis in Ethiopia’s Somali Regional State. The Moyale Clashes: A Somali Dimension The violence in Oromia directly affects ethnic Somali communities in Ethiopia. As reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the Moyale clashes , heavy fighting erupted between Oromo and Somali communities in the border town, killing at least nine people and forcing more than 2,500 Ethiopians to flee into Kenya. The trigger was a dispute over the display of the Somali Regional State flag at an administrative office in an area administered by Oromia. These clashes demonstrate how local disputes over flags, administrative boundaries, and political control can escalate into deadly confrontations with regional consequences. For Somalia, the displacement of ethnic Somalis across the border into Kenya carries humanitarian and security implications, particularly in a borderland region where Al-Shabaab has historically exploited instability. What This Means for Somalia: The Security Gap For Somalia, the implications are direct and urgent. Ethiopia’s internal conflicts are already drawing its military resources away from Somalia. As reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of Ethiopia’s military redeployment , Addis Ababa is planning to withdraw more than 3,000 troops from the Bay and Bakool regions of South West State to redeploy them to Tigray, Amhara, and Afar. This withdrawal would leave a security gap in areas where Ethiopian forces have been fighting Al-Shabaab, and it comes as the AUSSOM mission faces its own funding and mandate uncertainties. The timing is particularly delicate. The UN political mission in Somalia is closing its doors on October 31, ending more than three decades of international political stewardship. The AUSSOM mission faces a funding cliff and a potential withdrawal of Ugandan forces. As reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the transition , Somalia is entering a phase where it will have fewer international buffers and more direct responsibility for its own security. Ethiopia’s regional position is also hardening. As reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of Ethiopia’s response to the Alamein Declaration , Addis Ababa has rejected what it describes as “coercive measures” and “acts of destabilization” aimed at constraining its Red Sea ambitions. The four-nation Alamein Declaration, signed by Egypt, Eritrea, Somalia, and Sudan, formalized coordination on regional security and affirmed that Red Sea governance is the responsibility of littoral states. Ethiopia’s exclusion from that framework, combined with its internal conflicts, creates a volatile regional dynamic. Critical Note The massacre in Shirka is a crime that demands accountability, and the Ethiopian government’s failure to protect its citizens, particularly religious minorities, is a damning indictment of its security apparatus. The Orthodox Church’s statement that it had repeatedly raised concerns with authorities but received no solution is a familiar refrain in Ethiopia, where local communities have borne the brunt of conflicts that the state is either unable or unwilling to contain. For Somalia, the lesson is one of exposure. Ethiopia’s internal fragmentation is not a spectator sport. It is a process that is already reshaping the security architecture of the Horn of Africa. The withdrawal of Ethiopian troops from Somalia, the displacement of civilians across the Kenyan border, and the formation of a rebel alliance that includes armed groups from multiple regions all point in the same direction: Ethiopia is entering a period of prolonged instability, and Somalia will feel the consequences whether it is prepared or not. The Somali government’s focus on its own political crisis, the contested electoral process, and the fight against Al-Shabaab is understandable. But it cannot afford to ignore the collapse of order next door. The same international partners who are withdrawing from Somalia are also watching Ethiopia with concern. The same Al-Shabaab that Somalia is fighting has exploited Ethiopian instability in the past. The same borderlands that are now scenes of sectarian violence are the corridors through which weapons, fighters, and displaced people move. The Shirka massacre is a warning. It is not the first, and it will not be the last. Somalia’s security is not confined to its borders. It is shaped by the stability of its neighbors, and Ethiopia’s stability is deteriorating rapidly. The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church reported that the victims were targeted in attacks attributed to a newly formed rebel coalition, the Alliance for Survival, which includes the Oromo Liberation Army (OLA). Eyewitness accounts revealed that children were among the dead and numerous homes were destroyed. The situation underscores the interconnectedness of regional security, with Ethiopia's instability posing direct threats to Somalia's safety and political landscape.

ethiopia.title: All of Africa Today - October 27, 2026
ethiopia.content: Africa: All of Africa Today - October 27, 2026 - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Africa: All of Africa Today - October 27, 2026 AllAfrica AllAfrica logo 27 October 2026 allAfrica.com By Melody Chironda More Than 60 Killed In Attacks In Ethiopia More than 60 people have been killed in a series of attacks targeting Christian communities in Ethiopia's Oromia region, according to the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church. The attacks occurred in three areas of the Shirka district, where at least 20 houses were reportedly burnt down, and five children were among those killed. One resident described the violence as an ambush, saying attackers surrounded the community from all sides. A church official called the incident a massacre, adding that security forces arrived but were unable to stop the assault. Many residents have since fled the area. A local official blamed a newly formed rebel coalition, the Alliance for Survival, which includes the Oromo Liberation Army (OLA). The OLA has not commented on the latest allegations and previously denied responsibility for similar attacks. The Orthodox Church condemned the violence, saying attacks against Christians have increased and accusing authorities of failing to address repeated concerns about insecurity. A July 2026 report by the Ethiopian Human Rights Council recorded 458 deaths in attacks in the area over the previous four years, identifying local communities, particularly Orthodox Christians, as frequent targets. However, previous reports have also documented attacks against Muslims, with residents describing the violence as both ethnic and religious in nature. Algeria Approves Troop Deployment To Niger Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn Algeria is preparing to deploy troops to neighbouring Niger in its first foreign military deployment since sending forces to Egypt during the 1973 Arab-Israeli war. The proposed deployment follows a visit to Algiers by Niger's defence minister as the country seeks assistance in combating armed groups linked to al-Qaeda and Islamic State. Algeria's parliament approved the deployment, with 148 of 174 senators voting in favour before the lower house also backed the move. Algeria has not yet announced the timing or number of troops, but they are expected to help secure energy infrastructure in northern Niger, near the Libyan border. The operation would mark the first use of a 2020 constitutional provision permitting overseas military deployments and a significant departure from Algeria's longstanding opposition to sending troops abroad. Algerian officials have stressed that the mission is intended to protect economic infrastructure rather than wage war. The country has significant economic interests in Niger, including a proposed gas pipeline that would transport Nigerian gas through Niger to Algeria. UN Warns 3.6 Million in Uganda Facing Acute Food Insecurity as Crisis Worsens About 3.6 million people in Uganda face high levels of acute food insecurity, and the number is projected to rise to 4.4 million between February and June 2027, according to the 2026 Integrated Food Security Phase Classification report. Refugees and communities in the Karamoja sub-region are expected to face the greatest burden as food shortages and malnutrition worsen. The report estimates that 465,900 children under five and 246,300 pregnant and breastfeeding women will require treatment for acute malnutrition between April 2026 and March 2027. The crisis is being driven by recurring climate shocks, declining agricultural production, crop and livestock pests and diseases, high food prices, deteriorating livelihoods and limited access to healthcare, clean water, sanitation and social protection. United Nations Resident Coordinator in Uganda Leonard Zulu called for urgent action to protect vulnerable households and strengthen food systems before conditions deteriorate further. Prime Minister Robinah Nabbanja urged the government, development partners and humanitarian agencies to invest in sustainable solutions that enable communities to produce their own food and reduce dependence on emergency assistance. The assessment, conducted across 60 districts between August and September 2026, was launched alongside a $50 million joint appeal by the United Nations and its partners to support emergency responses in Karamoja and early interventions in 37 districts and eight refugee settlements. The proposed response includes cash assistance, agricultural and livestock support, nutrition screening and treatment, healthcare, child protection, gender-based violence prevention, water and sanitation programmes, and disaster preparedness. The report warns that without sustained investment and coordinated action, vulnerable communities could face worsening hunger and malnutrition in the coming months. Amnesty Warns Funding Crisis Could Shut Central African Republic War Crimes Court Amnesty International has warned that suspected perpetrators of war crimes and crimes against humanity in the Central African Republic (CAR), including senior officials, could escape justice if the country's Special Criminal Court (SCC) fails to secure urgent funding. In a report released in October 2026, the organisation said the court, inaugurated in 2018, has tried six cases and secured convictions against 19 people for war crimes and crimes against humanity, with reparations awarded to victims in one case. However, many survivors of atrocities committed during the 2003 coup and the 2012–2014 armed conflict are still waiting for those responsible to be prosecuted. The United States withdrew its funding in 2025, leaving more than US$4.15 million in unpaid commitments and plunging the court into an unprecedented financial crisis. The United Nations and European Union are now its only financial contributors, while funding shortages have forced staff reductions, including cuts to the witness protection unit, and prevented prosecutors from opening new investigations. Amnesty warned that the court could close when its mandate expires in October 2028 unless additional funding is secured. Ukraine Allegedly Supporting Mali Militia Ukraine is facing questions over its alleged involvement in supporting Tuareg fighters in northern Mali, a development that could extend its rivalry with Russia into Africa's Sahel region. A September 2026 CNN investigation reported that around 15 Ukrainian drone specialists were assisting Tuareg fighters, although DW said it had not independently verified the claims and Ukraine has not confirmed a specific operation. Analysts believe any involvement would fit Kyiv's broader strategy of weakening Russian influence internationally, particularly in countries where Moscow provides military support to governments. Mali's military authorities have increasingly relied on Russia for security assistance since taking power in coups in 2020 and 2021, with Russia's Africa Corps replacing the Wagner Group's role in 2025. Local officials attributed the assaults to a newly formed rebel coalition, the Alliance for Survival, which includes the Oromo Liberation Army (OLA). ethiopia.title: Ethiopia Delivers Over 1 Million Digital Business Registration, Licensing Services
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia Delivers Over 1 Million Digital Business Registration, Licensing Services - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia Delivers Over 1 Million Digital Business Registration, Licensing Services 26 October 2026 Ethiopian News Agency (Addis Ababa) Addis Ababa — Ethiopia provided more than 1.08 million business registration and licensing services digitally over a three-month period, according to the Ministry of Trade and Regional Integration. The milestone highlights ongoing national efforts to streamline business procedures and expand online public services. The ministry's latest online services report reveals that 1,088,787 services were delivered across federal institutions, regional states, and city administrations, underscoring the expanding role of digital platforms in the country's commercial administration. Among the regions, Oromia Regional State recorded the highest volume with 441,550 services provided. Addis Ababa followed with 204,512, Amhara with 156,193, and South Ethiopia with 101,891. By service category, trade name clearance accounted for the largest share, with 579,785 services delivered. Business license renewals followed with 122,730, while license amendments totaled 107,317. New business registrations accounted for 60,409 services. The ministry said the digital system was helping reduce bureaucratic burdens on the business community while improving the efficiency, accessibility and transparency of public service delivery. The expansion of digital business registration and licensing services is part of Ethiopia's broader digital transformation agenda, which aims to modernize public administration, simplify procedures and improve access to government services through technology. ethiopia.title: ICRC Reaffirms Commitment to Partnership With Ethiopia
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: ICRC Reaffirms Commitment to Partnership With Ethiopia - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: ICRC Reaffirms Commitment to Partnership With Ethiopia 26 October 2026 Ethiopian News Agency (Addis Ababa) Addis Ababa — The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) has reaffirmed its commitment to strengthening its partnership with Ethiopia, commending the humanitarian efforts of the Ethiopian Red Cross Society (ERCS). During discussions with President Taye Atske Selassie, ICRC Regional Director for Africa Mamadou Sow praised the ERCS for its humanitarian work across the country and emphasized the importance of international humanitarian law and strong leadership in ensuring that essential assistance reaches people in need. President Taye and Mamadou Sow discussed the validity and the importance of international humanitarian law. Sow also commended President Taye for promoting cooperation among key Ethiopian government institutions, including the Ministries of Health, Justice and Defense. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn He expressed appreciation for the access and acceptance granted to the ICRC in Ethiopia, which enable the organization to carry out its humanitarian operations. Highlighting the importance of collaboration with the ERCS, Sow described the organization as a key partner in implementing programs focused on water, health and food security across Ethiopia. "The Ethiopian Red Cross is a marvelous organization," Sow said. "It's our privileged partner in this country, with whom we work across Ethiopia on water, health, and food security." He also praised the ERCS's extensive volunteer network, describing volunteers as the backbone of the organization and the wider International Red Cross and Red Crescent Movement. "We are very proud of that partnership because it relies on so many volunteers who are the beating heart of our global movement," Sow added. "We take great pride in their work, as well as the strong support Ethiopia provides to its Red Cross society." Read the original article on ENA . ethiopia.title: Egypt to Deploy Troops in Somalia Under Bilateral Deal Ahead of Aussom Integration
ethiopia.content: Egypt to Deploy Troops in Somalia Under Bilateral Deal Ahead of Aussom Integration - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Egypt to Deploy Troops in Somalia Under Bilateral Deal Ahead of Aussom Integration 26 October 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) Addis Abeba — Egypt is preparing to deploy troops to Somalia under a bilateral military cooperation agreement before transferring approximately 1,000 personnel into the African Union Support and Stabilisation Mission in Somalia (AUSSOM), raising concerns over operational coordination and command structures. According to The East African report on 25 October, the initial deployment is expected to comprise a brigade-sized battle group with support elements in Middle Shabelle, north of Mogadishu. A tactical headquarters is planned at Ceelcade, near Ciciley airfield, an area currently held by Burundian AU troops. Additional Egyptian forces could be stationed elsewhere at Somalia's request, although Cairo has not disclosed the full size of its deployment. The African Union has yet to publicly clarify how the bilateral force will coordinate with AUSSOM and other contingents. Burundi's troops, which receive logistical support through the UN Support Office in Somalia (UNSOS), have reportedly not been formally notified of the proposed arrangements and have indicated they will not operate under a bilateral command structure. They are prepared to withdraw once replaced. Egypt was allocated approximately 1,091 troops under AUSSOM in late 2024 but delayed formal participation, citing funding constraints. Deploying under a bilateral agreement before integration raises questions over command authority, accountability, logistics and potential operational overlap. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn Egypt and Somalia signed a military cooperation agreement in August 2024, followed by Egyptian shipments of weapons, ammunition and armoured vehicles, as well as military training and advisory support. In August 2025, Somalia's Defence Ministry announced the completion of specialised training for Egyptian units intended for AUSSOM . A 16-member Egyptian military reconnaissance delegation visited Mogadishu the following month to assess deployment sites and logistics. Addis Standard previously reported o n preparations for the deployment , including troop movements and site work at Ceelcade, as formal integration remained delayed by funding and logistical challenges. The planned deployment comes as AUSSOM faces financial and operational pressures while supporting Somali forces against Al-Shabaab. Uncertainty over logistical support through UNSOS, amid questions about continued US funding, has further complicated the mission's sustainability. The move also carries regional implications amid longstanding tensions between Egypt and Ethiopia over the Nile waters and the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD), alongside competing interests in Red Sea access. ethiopia.summary: Egypt is set to deploy troops to Somalia under a bilateral military cooperation agreement, ahead of integrating approximately 1,000 personnel into the African Union Support and Stabilisation Mission in Somalia (AUSSOM). The initial deployment will consist of a brigade-sized battle group stationed in Middle Shabelle, with a tactical headquarters planned at Ceelcade, currently held by Burundian troops. Concerns have arisen regarding operational coordination and command structures, as the African Union has not clarified how the Egyptian forces will integrate with AUSSOM. Additionally, Burundi's troops have not been formally notified of the changes and are prepared to withdraw once replaced. Egypt's military cooperation with Somalia, which began in August 2024, includes weapon shipments and military training. The deployment comes amid financial pressures on AUSSOM and regional tensions, particularly between Egypt and Ethiopia over the Nile waters. Analysts warn that competing security partnerships could complicate Somalia's security arrangements. (159 words)

somalia.title: UN mission in Somalia to end operations on Oct. 31 after decades of support - Hiiraan Online
somalia.content: UN mission in Somalia to end operations on Oct. 31 after decades of support - Hiiraan Online Jobs | Twitter | Somali Links | RSS Dark Mode Hiiraan Online HOME OPINION POLITICS RSS CONTACT US FACEBOOK × OPINION WARARKA MAANTA SPORTS SECURITY POLITICS Privacy Policy Contact Us Jobs advertisements HOME SECURITY UN mission in Somalia to end operations on Oct. 31 after decades of support Share Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ Diyar Guldogan Tuesday October 27, 2026 'This milestone brings to a close more than three decades of United Nations missions in support of peacebuilding, state-building, governance and reconciliation in Somalia,’ says spokesman The UN Transitional Assistance Mission in Somalia (UNTMIS) will conclude its mandate on Oct. 31, ending a two-year transition and more than three decades of UN missions supporting peacebuilding, governance and state-building in the country, a UN official said Monday. In a statement, UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres’ spokesman, Stephane Dujarric, said the mission would cease operations in accordance with Security Council resolutions and a request from Somalia’s federal government. advertisements “This milestone brings to a close more than three decades of United Nations missions in support of peacebuilding, state-building, governance and reconciliation in Somalia,” Dujarric said. The closure follows a jointly agreed transition roadmap under which UNTMIS’s mandated responsibilities have been transferred to Somali institutions and UN agencies, funds and programmes. Guterres reaffirmed that the UN would continue supporting Somalia through its resident agencies and programmes, working with Somali authorities, the African Union and other international partners to promote peace, stability, human rights and sustainable development, Dujarric said. “Recognizing the significant political, security, humanitarian and development challenges that remain, the Secretary-General calls for sustained international support to consolidate progress, advance inclusive political dialogue and reconciliation, strengthen institutions, and promote and protect human rights,” he added. Dujarric stressed that Guterres reaffirmed the UN’s commitment to the people of Somalia and to supporting Somali-led efforts to build a peaceful, stable and prosperous future. somalia.summary: The United Nations Transitional Assistance Mission in Somalia (UNTMIS) will conclude its operations on October 31, marking the end of over three decades of UN involvement in the country. This decision follows a two-year transition period and aligns with requests from Somalia's federal government and Security Council resolutions. UN spokesman Stephane Dujarric emphasized that this milestone signifies the transfer of UNTMIS responsibilities to Somali institutions and various UN agencies. Despite the mission's closure, UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres assured continued support for Somalia through resident agencies, focusing on peace, stability, human rights, and sustainable development. He highlighted the ongoing political, security, and humanitarian challenges in the country, calling for sustained international support to foster political dialogue, reconciliation, and institutional strengthening. Guterres reaffirmed the UN's commitment to aiding Somalia in its efforts to achieve a peaceful and prosperous future.

somalia.title: US forces accused of ‘weaponising’ Somalia’s floods by trapping women and children in the path of El Niño - Hiiraan Online
somalia.content: US forces accused of ‘weaponising’ Somalia’s floods by trapping women and children in the path of El Niño - Hiiraan Online Jobs | Twitter | Somali Links | RSS Dark Mode Hiiraan Online HOME OPINION POLITICS RSS CONTACT US FACEBOOK × OPINION WARARKA MAANTA SPORTS SECURITY POLITICS Privacy Policy Contact Us Jobs advertisements HOME SECURITY US forces accused of ‘weaponising’ Somalia’s floods by trapping women and children in the path of El Niño Share Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ Mark Townsend in Kismayo Tuesday October 27, 2026 Exclusive: Coordinated airstrikes on territory held by al-Shabaab are driving the civilian population to find refuge alongside a river where rising water levels are a threat to safety. Is it a deliberate military strategy? A colonel from US special operations in Somalia with a soldier from a branch of the Somali army trained by US special forces, in Mogadishu in 2023. Photograph: Jonathan Torgovnik/Getty Images The water was rising rapidly. It had already reached Cayni Ali’s waist. Her home, five metres from the flooded River Juba in southern Somalia, never stood a chance. There was nowhere to go. Ali’s city of Jilib was under attack. Repeated airstrikes, said the mother of six, were pinning its population beside the rising river. “The drones come all the time,” said the 27-year-old. “We hear them constantly. They kill animals, civilians. The town is big but destruction is everywhere.” Asho Omar from Malenda, a village near Jilib, described “constant” airstrikes that had forced people towards the banks of the Juba. advertisements “The airstrikes are everywhere; it is difficult to move. So many people have been killed.” Their testimony offers a rare glimpse of life inside the stronghold of al-Shabaab, the Islamist militants who control 30% of Somalia. Closed off from the outside world, residents describe a city dealing with significant civilian casualties. Bodies, some said, lay in the streets. The ongoing conflict is a legally ambiguous, shadowy war coordinated by the United States in east Africa, in which there is little accountability for harm to Somali civilians. The United States Africa Command (Africom) would not share “operational security” details of a seemingly accelerating campaign that has also raised questions over potential covert US strikes. But there is, perhaps, an even darker dimension to the offensive on al-Shabaab’s de facto capital. Sources say the military strategy appears to be seeking to drown those living in al-Shabaab territory by “weaponising” a rapidly strengthening El Niño, forecast to intensify Somalia’s rainy season from this month. An aerial view of the Juba River, close to the town of Kismayo. Photograph: Hugh Kinsella Cunningham “The airstrikes are forcing people to go close to the river. It’s an extremely aggressive offensive, exploiting El Niño as a weapon of war to push the population into flood-prone areas,” said a source monitoring the Juba floodplain in southern Somalia. Pinning the population – which includes large numbers of women and children – on the river’s floodplain has raised concerns of large-scale deaths in the months ahead. “The official line is that they are targeting military positions and al-Shabaab, but because al-Shabaab is embedded within the community, it’s difficult to avoid collateral damage,” added the source. When El Niño last struck Somalia in 2023, it caused the worst floods seen in the country for a century, displacing more than 1.2 million people. Analysts have questioned the ethics of the US military allegedly using mapping data from flood-prone areas – conceived to mitigate civilian casualties – to inflict harm. Jethro Norman, a senior researcher with the Danish Institute for International Studies, said: “A weaponisation of El Niño is a reversal of process – using humanitarian remote sensing to inflict casualties rather than to mitigate harm. You capture the cumulative impact of a sustained airstrikes campaign in an El Niño flooding context.” US officials deny exploiting climatic factors. A spokesperson said: “Africom does not target civilians, conduct operations for the purpose of displacing civilian populations or use weather or flooding as a method of warfare. Africom targets lawful military objectives and takes feasible measures to mitigate civilian harm.” Nevertheless, many wonder if the opportunity to weaken al-Shabaab using the weather was too tempting to ignore, offering a catastrophic drowning event blamed on a supercharged El Niño. Like many cities, Jilib’s location has been found wanting in an era of extreme weather. On a low-lying plain, the city is chronically vulnerable to flooding. In 2023, vast swathes of farmland were submerged. Halimo Abdikadir from Kamsuuma, south of Jillib, described the destruction of her home, 6 miles (10km) from the river. “The waters came quickly at night – when they left, everything was mud. A lot of animals drowned.” Arbey Famu from Ahmed Yare, another village outside Jilib, expects this El Niño to be far worse than 2023: her crops of maize and sorghum are underwater. “In Jilib, there is big flooding already,” said the 70-year-old. US defence officials will know the early indicators of El Niño’s impact in al-Shabaab’s heartland. UN agencies say the Juba River basin is of “particular concern”. The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), meanwhile, foresees “severe flooding”. Attacking Jilib using ground forces carries much risk. Airstrikes can yield triumphs such as the death of a senior al-Shabaab commander on 1 October, but are unable to overrun a city of 100,000. Ali Adan Ali, the commissioner for displaced people in Jubaland, is worried. In his Kismayo office, Ali identified 327 regions prone to flooding. By October, El Niño warnings had only been issued to half. His chief concern is the lack of boats. Without them, he says, thousands in al-Shabaab territory risk being trapped on the east side of the river, unable to reach help in Kismayo, at the mouth of the Juba. Three years ago, during the last El Niño, Ali says, 19,000 people were stranded for a week without food. “We are running out of time,” he says. The absence of boats sums up Somalia’s funding woes. In 2023, the country’s aid budget was $2.2bn. Now it stands at about $300,000. Flood protection investment has dwindled. Compounding concerns is al-Shabaab’s lack of preparedness in the area it controls. Ali has not received a response from the militants regarding El Niño readiness. Cayni Ali said there are no sandbags or flood defences deployed yet in Jilib. Earth walls were erected along the river but have proved insufficient. “They are not big enough,” she said. The latest flood advisory for the River Juba urges communities to “reinforce” weak riverbanks. Corroborating testimonies describe a prolonged – and seemingly indiscriminate – campaign of airstrikes against al-Shabaab that appears to have killed many civilians. The US would not share details of potential civilian fatalities “to protect US and partner forces and preserve operational security”. Farhan Ahmed, who lived in Jilib until fleeing last month, described constant terror. “There were airstrikes every day, all the time.” One strike flattened five homes in his neighbourhood. Ahmed, 35, described bodies littering the city streets. Fadumo Abdi claimed the airstrikes were largely failing to target militants. “The attacks are mostly killing civilians. Some were buried, but some were not,” she said. Abdikadir, from Kamsuuma, added: “The drone attacks on Jilib are too much. So many people die.” Yusuf Siidi, 27, from Araare near Jamame in al-Shabaab territory, witnessed three teenagers killed in one strike. Maryan Salah was at home near Jamame when a drone sent a shard of burning metal 20cm long into her back yard, landing next to her two-year-old daughter. “It was so close. I am very angry. I’m not part of the conflict.” Salah’s near miss predates the current offensive. She can recall only that it happened in “mid-March”. The US admits a drone strike near Jamame on 19 March, but no other data is provided. Although eyewitness accounts detail an extraordinary number of strikes in Jilib, official US records confirm only one airstrike in Jilib during August. Six took place last month. Between the start of August and now, the US says it conducted a total of just 11 strikes. Allegations of ambiguity increasingly characterise US operations in Somalia. It is an opaque approach that raises questions over whether Africom has authorised covert airstrikes in the region. Records from the nearest hospital indicate intensive airstrikes or fighting. The ICRC has treated 205 patients with “weapon-related” injuries in Kismayo this year, a 43% increase on last year. David Sterman, analyst at the New America thinktank, said: “The possibility that we are seeing covert US strikes always looms large when there are strikes without clear attribution.” The US, however, said it publicised “all airstrikes conducted under its authority in Somalia. We do not maintain an undisclosed or unannounced strike count.” Turkey has also used drones to target al-Shabaab in Somalia. Operating alongside Africom, Turkey rarely divulges any details of its strikes or military operations in Somalia. Beyond airstrikes and floods, the primary concern for Somalis is hunger. Those fleeing the Juba valley – local authorities are offering humanitarian help to those who escape – say there is insufficient food to sustain them. Omar’s family of 13 survives on one fish a day. How big is the fish? Omar held her hands less than 30cm apart. Habiba Ali, 55, from Jamame, said her family – like many – shares one daily meal of maize. Time in between is spent hiding from conflict. “When the fighting stops, we wait for it start again.” In Kismayo, too, long-term drought and USAID cuts have brought misery. Shukri Ahmed, 32, the president of Galbeed refugee camp, estimates that 6,000 might have died in Kismayo’s network of displacement sites since the Trump administration abruptly shut USAID last year. Overnight, two children had died in makeshift shelters from diarrhoea. El Niño will “deepen [Somalia’s] hunger levels”, warns the UN-backed body responsible for identifying famine. Fadumo Abdi with her 14-month-old baby, Maryan, in the infant intensive-care unit in Kismayo hospital. Photograph: Hugh Kinsella Cunningham Zakaria Mohammed, head nurse at Kismayo’s ICRC-supported hospital for five years, says children from al-Shabaab territory arrive every day so severely malnourished or weak they cannot be saved. Cases of child malnutrition rates have risen 40% this year. Xaawo Nacdoor made it just in time. Al-Shabaab had blocked her leaving Jamame to receive treatment for her baby. But her 14-month-old daughter Faadumo was dying, so Nacdoor fled at night. For three days, with just a bottle of water, Nacdoor walked with her daughter strapped to her back. On the second day, the toddler lost consciousness. “She was severely dehydrated, but I kept going.” Arriving at the hospital, Faadumo weighed 4.1kg. Three days later: 4.4kg. She survived. Most patients here vow never to return home, saying life under al-Shabaab meant no school, education, healthcare or food. For the thousands of families straddling the Juba River – often the poorest – things are about to get much worse. somalia.summary: US forces are facing accusations of "weaponising" floods in Somalia by conducting airstrikes that force civilians, particularly women and children, towards the flood-prone banks of the Juba River. As El Niño intensifies the rainy season, residents in areas like Jilib report constant airstrikes that have devastated their communities and left them with no safe refuge. Eyewitness accounts describe significant civilian casualties, with many bodies left in the streets. Critics argue that the US military strategy appears to exploit the flooding to weaken al-Shabaab, the militant group controlling much of the region. Although US officials deny targeting civilians or using weather as a weapon, the situation raises ethical concerns about the military's operations and the potential for large-scale humanitarian crises. With inadequate flood defenses and dwindling resources, the looming threat of severe flooding exacerbates the already dire conditions for those living in al-Shabaab territory, where hunger and displacement are rampant.

Privacy Policy Terms of Service Search Hassan Anwar Carries Somalia’s Boxing Hopes to the Youth Olympics in Senegal October 27, 2026 3 min read HW By Hassan Wekesa - Editor 27 October 2026 - When young boxers step into the ring at the Youth Olympic Games in Dakar, Senegal, Somalia and Kenya will have one thing in common. Somalia pins its hopes of a medal in the male category on 17-year-old Hassan Anwar Mohamed, while Kenya banks on Ellah Edemesi, a promising 16-year-old, in the female category. The only difference is how the two started boxing. Hassan says he was motivated from the very beginning, while Edemesi was not initially obsessed with the sport. Hassan Anwar Mohamed of Somalia Hassan’s coach, Mohamed Ahmed Abdullahi, says his boxer is ready for the competition. “We will show people who we are,” he said as he trained the younger boxer at Mecca Gym, located at Eastleigh's 4th Street in Nairobi. The draw for the Dakar bouts has not yet been released, so Hassan’s opponents will be known soon. Mohamed holds 1-Star certificates from the International Olympic Committee (IOC), the International Boxing Association (IBA) and World Athletics, and he still boxes himself. He said Hassan has trained at camps in Somalia, Sierra Leone and Kenya. “We are very happy to be here in Nairobi. We enjoy the conducive climate here,” he said. Asked whether there were opponents from specific countries the Somali boxer would wish to avoid in the early stages, the coach said no boxer worth their salt would have such an attitude. “Our player is ready to battle it out with his opponents,” he said. Somali Boxing Association President Awil Gele Ahmed said the country’s boxing has continued to grow since 2018, although sponsorship has not been as expected. “Many corporates are still reluctant to support boxing in our country,” Awil said. Related articles Guelleh Announces $10 million For Young Entrepreneurs in Djibouti Somalia Launches Cybersecurity Push as 4th National Forum Opens in Mogadishu He added that Hassan’s role model is former British featherweight world champion Prince Naseem Hamed. Hassan, who competes in the 50kg category, is very excited to represent his country in boxing as he prepares to leave for Dakar. The Games kick off on 31 October 2026. Hassan together with his managers is expected to leave for Senegal on Wednesday. The intense training including shadow boxing and spurring, have helped him fine-tune techniques. With the 2028 Los Angeles Olympic Games also coming up, Somalia Boxing Association President said the qualifiers are coming up in January 2027 and that home boxers are ready. Ellah Edemesi of Kenya Edemesi says that whenever she steps into the ring, two fighters occupy a special place in her mind. The first is Kenya’s Veronica Mbithe of the Kenya Defence Forces, whose unique boxing style captivates her. The second is American professional boxer Claressa Shields, whom Edemesi admires not only for her ability in the ring but also for the difficult journey she overcame to reach the top. Shields’ story resonates with her. Shields started boxing young, persevered through hardship and, at a time when few girls were involved in the sport, found a way to pursue her dream. For Edemesi, that resilience is a reminder that obstacles do not have to define her future. Together, the two role models inspire the teenager as she heads towards her ambitious destination, the Youth Olympic Games in Dakar. Her own journey into boxing, however, was not born from an early obsession with the sport. It began almost by accident. Edemesi, a student at Shadrack Kimalel Senior School in Nairobi, started boxing in 2024 after repeatedly watching her younger brother, Ramsey Wakhu. Ramsey, 14, was already a boxer, and his bouts gradually sparked her curiosity. “At first, I just went to watch my brother’s boxing bouts so as to pass time,” Edemesi said. Somalia’s 17-year-old Hassan Anwar Mohamed trains in Nairobi for his 50kg Youth Olympic Games bouts in Dakar, Senegal. somalia.summary: Hassan Anwar Mohamed, a 17-year-old boxer from Somalia, is set to represent his country at the Youth Olympic Games in Dakar, Senegal, starting on October 31, 2026. Competing in the 50kg category, Hassan is seen as Somalia's best hope for a medal, with his coach, Mohamed Ahmed Abdullahi, expressing confidence in his readiness for the competition. Hassan has trained extensively in Somalia, Sierra Leone, and Kenya, honing his skills under the guidance of experienced coaches. Meanwhile, Kenya's Ellah Edemesi, a 16-year-old boxer, also prepares for her bouts, inspired by role models like Claressa Shields. Both athletes highlight the growth of boxing in their respective countries, despite challenges such as a lack of sponsorship. The Somali Boxing Association President noted the sport's development since 2018, while Hassan looks forward to showcasing his talent on an international stage. The upcoming Games are also seen as a stepping stone towards the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.

somalia.title: Somalia reports deadly fighting with Al-Shabaab as both sides claim heavy losses - AOL.co.uk
somalia.content: Somalia reports deadly fighting with Al-Shabaab as both sides claim heavy losses - AOL Skip to main content Advertisement Animals Entertainment Games Horoscopes Lifestyle Money News UK Sport Cricket F1 Football Golf Tennis Other Sports Weather Amazon Deals Menu Sign in Email Help Email Sign in Animals Entertainment Games Horoscopes Lifestyle Money News UK Sport Cricket F1 Football Golf Tennis Other Sports Weather Amazon Deals Sign in Animals Entertainment Games Horoscopes Lifestyle Money News UK Sport Cricket F1 Football Golf Tennis Other Sports Weather Amazon Deals Help Somalia reports deadly fighting with Al-Shabaab as both sides claim heavy losses RFI Tue, October 27, 2026 at 4:10 PM UTC 0 (AP - Farah Abdi Warsameh) The Somali defence ministry said on Tuesday that federal troops had killed 75 militants and wounded 56 others. The Al-Qaeda-linked insurgent group claimed it had killed 321 government soldiers during an attack on Turkish-trained troops and an allied militia. Neither account could be independently verified, leaving the scale of the casualties unclear. The fighting took place in the Lower Shabelle region , where the government is battling an insurgency that has endured for two decades despite a major international effort to defeat it. Somalia sets date for May presidential election amid ongoing Islamist insurgency Conflicting accounts of the battle Al-Shabaab said it launched its attack on Monday afternoon, describing a three-hour ambush in which its fighters also captured prisoners, weapons and vehicles. The defence ministry presented the fighting as an offensive against militant positions. “The Somali National Army, conducting Operation Banooda , launched a major assault lasting several hours on 26 October against Al-Shabaab positions in Jameeca,” it said in a statement. The government confirmed that militants had used vehicles packed with explosives during the attack and acknowledged damage to military equipment. “The attack damaged some military vehicles,” the ministry said. Its statement did not provide a toll for government forces or confirm Al-Shabaab’s claims to have taken prisoners and seized equipment. Local media platform Baidoa Online reported that the government had called an emergency cabinet meeting to discuss what it described as “heavy casualties and substantial military equipment losses” during the fighting near Leego. That report added to indications of a significant confrontation, although the competing claims offered no independently verified picture of how the battle unfolded or which side suffered the greater losses. Turkey expands military footprint in Somalia as regional rivalries intensify Pressure on international support The clashes come as Somalia’s government faces uncertainty over international backing for its campaign against Al-Shabaab, which continues to control large areas of central Somalia. Turkey has emerged as a key supporter of the federal government, including through the training of Somali troops. Its role has become increasingly important as the US and other major donors pull back from supporting the counter-insurgency effort. Washington has stopped funding the United Nations logistics mission that supplies combat operations in Somalia – a vital part of the international support underpinning the campaign. The US has cited the government’s failure to make progress in uniting the country and confronting the insurgent threat as its reason for ending that funding. The withdrawal adds pressure on Somali forces and their partners as they seek to sustain operations against a group that remains capable of mounting major attacks.
